title: The Hoax
full_review:
"The Hoax" (Miramax) is an imaginative, but only fitfully involving, riff on the claims by real-life author Clifford Irving (Richard Gere in excellent form) to have the exclusive rights to eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes' autobiography back in the early 1970s.

What starts as an almost offhanded prank -- after his editor, the fictitiously named Andrea Tate (Hope Davis), informs him his novel has been rejected (not true in life) -- takes on headline-making proportions. He's aided by his friend, writing partner and reluctant co-conspirator Dick Susskind (an amusing Alfred Molina as Irving's quivering voice of conscience), and European artist wife Edith (Marcia Gay Harden), who sticks by him even when she learns of his adulterous affair with Baroness (and later actress) Nina Van Pallandt (Julie Delpy).

The skeptical top brass at publisher McGraw-Hill -- led by president Shelton Fisher (Stanley Tucci) -- let themselves believe Irving can deliver the goods, agreeing to pay him a million dollars.

As Irving dreams up increasingly ingenious ways to prevent the truth from leaking, his and Susskind's apprehension of being caught builds into extreme paranoia, even to the point of their fleeing down the emergency exit stairs at McGraw-Hill.

The facts of this case are already so unbelievable that the film's embellishments are scarcely necessary. And William Wheeler's overly complex and fanciful script includes such questionable elements as Susskind having an affair with a hooker and Irving physically stealing the manuscript of the unpublished Hughes biography which he, in part, plagiarized.

The film dramatizes a cloak-and-dagger meeting with an emissary from Hughes who indicates the big man is willing to cooperate, in exchange for Irving including some incriminating information on President Richard Nixon.
There seems to be good evidence to suggest that Nixon really may have worried that the manuscript contained a revelation about Nixon's brother getting illegal loans from Hughes in exchange for favors. Nixon's fears, the film contends, may have led to the Watergate break-in and ultimately his own downfall.

This change of pace from director Lasse Hallstrom sometimes resembles George Clooney's "Confessions of a Dangerous Mind" in its truth-vs.-reality structure, and is sometimes confusing.

The film doesn't glamorize Irving's scheme (ultimately exposed when Hughes disowned the book in a press conference via telephone), but rather shows the extreme mental anguish Irving -- who spent two and a half years in prison -- brought on himself.

The film contains considerable rough language and profanity, crude expressions, an adulterous affair, an encounter with a prostitute, and some sexual talk and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
